body.text: The threat below the waterline in Cambodia and Thailand’s truce
Confidence-building measures for conciliation are a first step, but the harder part is interpreting all the other messages.

A bid to resolve Cambodia and Thailand maritime dispute is underway. After five days of talks in The Hague, the parties this week agreed to a list of confidence-building measures. The Conciliation Commission, chaired by Australian diplomat Katrina Cooper, asked both sides to show restraint in public statements, appoint senior envoys to each other’s capitals and join a technical working group on delimitation.

But there is ambiguity. The conciliation is proceeding under Annex V of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the outcome will not bind either party. A non-binding process succeeds when every actor able to wreck it chooses not to – and that list runs well beyond the two foreign ministries at the table.

After the Thai cabinet this year cancelled a 2001 memorandum covering overlapping claims, Cambodia initiated the conciliation. The Commission met in Singapore on 14–16 September, in The Hague on 14–18 October, and is due to meet again in Kuala Lumpur on 24–27 November.
Sub-threshold pressure could pose challenges to the procedure.
The opening session of the Conciliation Commission on 15 September (PCA-CPA)

The first risk is that either side attempts to change facts at sea while the conciliation process keeps arguing. On 9 and 12 February, swarms of 25 to 30 fishing boats from Cambodia entered waters off Koh Kut, prompting warning shots from a Thai warship and a statement that “This is the Thai sea”.

On 14 February a Cambodian naval unit detained a Thai boat off Koh Kong, which some in the Thai government considered to be retaliation. Bangkok’s own instruments, cancelling the memorandum, keeping checkpoints shut and freezing the Joint Boundary Commission, are coercion by administrative means.

Each incremental move could distract the conciliation process. Both governments should treat fishing surges, retaliatory detentions and procedural walkouts as breaches of the process, and route incidents through the local border committee rather than the press.

Another risk is the provocation at home made by the military. The Hague measures address “the Parties” referring whole governments, not just diplomatic missions. The measures commit both sides to restraint in statements that could inflame public sentiment. Thai commanders had earlier forecast a third round of fighting. In March, the army’s intelligence chief, Lt Gen Theeranan Nanthakwang, warned of a coming clash in the months after the rainy season, a window that opens about now. In June, the Second Army Area commander, Lt Gen Weerayuth Raksilp, said renewed fighting would favour “whoever is better prepared, faster, better armed”. The navy chief has declared his force “100% ready”, and a retired senior commander insisted in January that a third round will happen.

Cambodia’s defence ministry rejects claims it is readying for conflict. Still, when generals forecast war while their foreign minister negotiates, Cambodian planners might conclude that the military, not the diplomats, hold the veto.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul should make clear that public talk of renewed fighting contradicts commitments Thailand has now accepted in The Hague – Phnom Penh should do likewise.

Military procurement also sends different signals. Within a week of the Singapore session, Thailand selected a bidder for a THB16.7 billion (A$708 million) frigate and approved another THB3.5 billion for missiles, artillery and replacement equipment, partly to supply future operations.

Thailand says the frigate replaces ageing vessels and was specified by mission, not by country. That is plausible, but where no boundary exists, new capability reads as intent. Events on land, where the border is also disputed, have an effect too. Thai commanders cite reported Cambodian tank movements, claims Cambodia’s defence ministry rejected, saying it has proposed that neither side threaten or use force at sea.

Confidence-building measures are welcome, but trust will be hard won. Maintaining transparency at sea, avoiding provocation and escaping the security dilemma through procurement are the practicable ways forward. The Commission can propose a boundary, but only governments, with their armed forces, fleets and media in line, can adopt an effective result.
